THE PANDEMIC PROFITS INVESTIGATION

THE £6.67 MILLION LABOUR COVID TESTING SCANDAL

A former Labour councillor convicted. A former Labour MP and justice minister acquitted. A second councillor, formerly Labour and once the MP’s parliamentary office manager, also cleared. False Covid results, million-pound transfers and a financial trail demanding answers.
BY STEVE ENGLISH   |   BRITISH LIONS ROAR   |   10 OCTOBER 2026

While Britain lived under Covid restrictions, a Halifax testing laboratory was generating millions of pounds. Customers trusted the results. Some received negative certificates even though their samples had not been properly tested. The eventual criminal case revealed a web of politically connected business figures, contested financial transfers and questions that reach far beyond one laboratory.

THE TESTS WERE SUPPOSED TO PROTECT THE PUBLIC. SOME NEGATIVE RESULTS WERE ISSUED WITHOUT TESTING THE SAMPLES.
01 / INVESTIGATION

THE LABOUR CONNECTIONS

Faisal Shoukat, a former Labour councillor for Calderdale’s Park ward and a pharmacist, was convicted of fraudulent trading, causing a public nuisance and money laundering. Shahid Malik, a former Labour MP for Dewsbury and former government justice minister, co-founded RT Diagnostics and was acquitted of all three charges. Paul Moore, Malik’s former parliamentary office manager and a Kirklees councillor who had been suspended by Labour and sat as an independent, was also acquitted. Manager Lynn Connell and clinical director Alexander Zarneh were acquitted. No Labour membership has been established for Connell or Zarneh. These are documented personal political connections, not evidence that the Labour Party itself owned or operated the laboratory.

02 / INVESTIGATION

A LABORATORY ISSUING FALSE NEGATIVES

RT Diagnostics began offering general-population tests in April 2021 and expanded into travel PCR testing in May. Prosecutors described a business that took on more samples than it could process, employed young staff with inadequate training and allowed returned tests to accumulate unprocessed. Some customers were given negative results without their samples being tested. Between 21 May and 21 July 2021, 138,738 PCR results were reported, with just 45 positives — approximately 0.032%. The figure is a reported result rate, not an independently verified infection rate. False negatives could have allowed infected customers to travel or mix with others in the belief they had tested negative.

03 / INVESTIGATION

THE PREMISES AND THE VIDEO

Footage published by The Sun in July 2021 showed disordered laboratory premises and unprocessed samples. It became part of the wider public account of the operation. The court found serious failures and criminal conduct by Shoukat. The judge did not find that the business was necessarily founded with the original intention of issuing false results: the operation became overwhelmed, and false reporting became part of how it functioned.

04 / INVESTIGATION

THE £6.67 MILLION AND THE SECOND COMPANY

Court reporting described revenue of approximately £6.67 million over a short period in 2021. Prosecutors said a second entity, Real Time Diagnostics Ltd, with a name strikingly similar to RT Diagnostics, held the account into which business revenue was paid. The Crown questioned the arrangement and the subsequent movement of funds. The defence disputed that the second company or its bank account was inherently improper, explaining that the original business had encountered difficulties obtaining banking facilities. Those competing accounts must not be confused with a finding that every transfer was criminal.

05 / INVESTIGATION

THE PAYMENTS: £1.22 MILLION AND £822,000

The trial heard of substantial transfers, including approximately £1.22 million to accounts belonging to Malik and £822,000 to Halifax Healthcare, a company associated with Shoukat. Reports also described dividend payments to Malik totalling just under £1.5 million by August 2021. These figures may overlap: dividends, account transfers and share interests cannot simply be added together as if they were separate profits. Malik’s defence maintained the payments were legitimate dividends from a profitable business. He was acquitted of money laundering and the other charges.

06 / INVESTIGATION

WHAT THE JUDGE SAID ABOUT MALIK

In reporting on the judge’s subsequent reasons, Judge Christopher Smith was said to have expressed a “very real suspicion” about what Malik knew when newspaper footage emerged and the timing of substantial dividends. But suspicion was not proof of knowledge of false test results. The judge concluded that the criminal case against Malik had not been established, and Malik was acquitted. Reporting the judge’s concern and the acquittal together is essential to understanding the outcome.

07 / INVESTIGATION

AVERY LABS: THE PROSECUTION’S REPLACEMENT THEORY

Avery Labs Limited was incorporated in June 2021 as RT Diagnostics was facing regulatory problems. Prosecutors alleged that it was intended to take over testing activity and revive the revenue stream, with Moore prominent in the new venture and financial links to the earlier business. The defence challenged that interpretation and described a different commercial purpose. The company was subsequently dissolved in May 2024. Its incorporation did not establish that it committed a crime; Moore and Malik were acquitted.

08 / INVESTIGATION

THE SCIENTIST AND THE APPROVAL PROCESS

Alexander Zarneh was the registered scientist associated with clinical oversight. The prosecution questioned the information provided in connection with approval and accreditation. Zarneh was acquitted. The case nonetheless raises serious public-interest questions about how provider listings, actual laboratory capacity, accreditation status, sample handling and quality assurance were checked during the rapid expansion of pandemic testing.

09 / INVESTIGATION

THE TRIAL WITHOUT A JURY

The lengthy Bradford Crown Court proceedings took an extraordinary turn when the jury was discharged following an allegation of jury tampering. The judge continued without a jury and determined the verdicts. Shoukat challenged the procedure, but the Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal that ruling. An allegation concerning a juror is not evidence that any defendant, lawyer or judge participated in jury tampering.

10 / INVESTIGATION

WHERE DID THE REST OF THE MONEY GO?

The reported revenue, personal transfers and associated-company payments do not amount to a complete forensic accounting. The unanswered questions include how much remained in company accounts, what was spent on operating costs, how much was retained by shareholders, whether customers received refunds and whether confiscation or compensation proceedings have recovered any proceeds. The public deserves a documented reconciliation, not a speculative total.

11 / INVESTIGATION

THE QUESTIONS THAT STILL DEMAND ANSWERS

Who approved the provider listing and what checks were performed? When did regulators learn that samples were not being properly processed? How many customers received false results? What was the full transaction history of the second company’s account? What funding did Avery Labs actually receive? Were any dividends or assets recovered? And what safeguards now prevent a similar breakdown? The criminal verdict resolves Shoukat’s liability; it does not answer every regulatory and financial question.

12 / INVESTIGATION

THE VERDICT — AND THE WIDER SCANDAL

During a national emergency, people paid for medical tests and relied on certificates that should have been trustworthy. In this case, the court convicted a former Labour councillor of serious offences arising from a laboratory that issued false results. Other politically connected figures were involved in the business and were acquitted. The facts are substantial enough without inventing guilt: a multimillion-pound operation, alarming testing failures, a disputed corporate money trail, and unresolved questions about oversight and recovery. The court case is over for the acquitted defendants. The public-interest investigation should not be.
